coffees.name: China Yunnan Black Sheep Double Anaerobic
coffees.processNote: This one is the odd sheep of the month, and the name is honest about it. The cherries are dried partway, then sealed whole into tanks with the oxygen shut out for about three weeks, then dried again to finish. Two rounds of fermentation is where the booze and the spice come from, and it is a lot. Roast it light and the cup goes wild and fruity. Push it to a strong medium and it turns toward rum, oak, and cocoa. Either way, strong fermentation is not for everyone, and I would rather tell you that now than have you wonder what happened to your mug.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Most people do not picture China when they picture coffee, but Yunnan has been growing it for over a century, since French missionaries planted the first trees in the 1890s, and today nearly all of China's coffee comes from these mountains. Ximeng is a Wa autonomous county in the far southwest of Pu'er, the prefecture better known the world over for its tea, hard against the border with Myanmar. The Wa farms here sit between 1,400 and 1,600 meters in steep, wet, forested hills, and the Catimor they grow was planted for its toughness against leaf rust, which is exactly why it needs processing this bold to show what it can do.

Torch Coffee has worked out of Pu'er for over a decade, started by an American coffee educator named Marty Pollack and his partners, and it runs a roasting floor, a lab, and a training school that teaches the farmers around it to cup their own coffee. Their whole approach is crop to cup, which in Yunnan means fixing the part between the farm and the port that used to swallow all the quality. Black Sheep is their experiment lot, the one that breaks every rule the washed Yunnan coffees follow, and I brought it in because I have never tasted anything from China like it.

journey.label: Ximeng · Pu'er, Yunnan, China
journey.story: This is about as far from Oberlin as coffee grows. Ximeng is Wa country, a county of forested ridges in the southwest corner of Yunnan where the hills run straight on into Myanmar's Shan State. The Wa farms sit between 1,400 and 1,600 meters, wet most of the year, and the coffee leaves through Pu'er, the city that gave its name to the famous aged tea. To the west the border hills climb toward the Awa Mountains.

lookArounds.label: Walk the Great Wall
lookArounds.note: The Great Wall at Mutianyu, in the mountains about 70 kilometers northeast of Beijing. This stretch is Ming dynasty, built in the 1400s on an older foundation, with 22 watchtowers along a ridge of about two kilometers. It is a long way from the coffee, nearly the whole length of the country, but you cannot come to China and not walk it. Drag to look around; the arrows move you along the wall.

lookArounds.label: Downtown Kunming
lookArounds.note: Kunming, the capital of Yunnan, called the Spring City for weather that stays mild all year at 1,900 meters. These are the Golden Horse and Jade Rooster archways in the middle of downtown, where the streets fill up at night. Every coffee that leaves Yunnan by air comes through here.

coffees.name: Kenya Nyeri Rui Ruiru Anaerobic Natural
coffees.processNote: Kenya built its reputation on washed coffee, which uses a lot of water, and water is getting precious in the hills. This lot skips the washing entirely. The whole cherries go into sealed tanks with no oxygen for about six days, then onto raised beds where they dry in the fruit for close to a month. The fruit cooks the sugar into the seed, so what you get is red berry jam and bright orange instead of the blackcurrant you may expect from Kenya, with a dark chocolate base that gets deeper the further you take the roast.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Nyeri sits in the high country between Mount Kenya and the Aberdare Range, on red volcanic soil that is about as good as coffee dirt gets. Rui Ruiru is a factory, which is what Kenyans call a washing station, in the Mathira area east of Nyeri town, taking cherry from a few hundred smallholders who each farm a small patch of trees between 1,800 and 2,000 meters. The varieties are the Kenyan classics, SL28 and SL34, the ones that give the country its bright, juicy reputation, plus Ruiru 11, bred locally for disease resistance.

The factory has a comeback story. The cooperative that ran it folded in 2014 and the place was left to fall apart for years. In 2020 the farmers around it, led by the village headman, got backing from the county and the Ministry of Agriculture and partnered with a group called Crowd Farm Africa to rebuild it and bring the cherry back. Torch Coffee, the same Yunnan outfit behind this month's China lot, has been working with them on these anaerobic naturals, which is how a tiny revived station in Nyeri ended up doing some of the most experimental processing in Kenya.

journey.label: Rui Ruiru · Mathira, Nyeri, Kenya
journey.story: Nyeri is where Kenyan coffee started earning its name, in the saddle of high ground between Mount Kenya and the Aberdares, almost exactly on the equator. The Rui Ruiru factory sits in Mathira, where a few hundred smallholders bring cherry down from trees planted in red volcanic soil at close to 2,000 meters. Straight ahead, the glaciers of Mount Kenya climb past 5,000 meters.

lookArounds.label: Drive the Maasai Mara
lookArounds.note: The Maasai Mara National Reserve, 1,500 square kilometers of open savanna in the southwest of the country that runs on into the Serengeti. Every year from about July to October more than a million wildebeest cross the Mara River here on the Great Migration, with the crocodiles waiting. Google drove the tracks of the reserve in 2019, so the arrows let you drive it too. Look for the lions.

lookArounds.label: Stand on Mount Kenya
lookArounds.note: Point Lenana, the trekking summit of Mount Kenya at 4,985 meters, with the twin rock peaks of Batian and Nelion above it. The Kikuyu call the mountain Kirinyaga and the coffee grows on its lower slopes, so this is the view from above the farms. One local-shot 360 from the top.

lookArounds.label: Nairobi, with the giraffes
lookArounds.note: Nairobi National Park, the only national park on earth inside a capital city. Giraffes, rhinos, and lions graze with the downtown skyline on the horizon, a few minutes from the airport this coffee flew out of.

coffees.name: Guatemala Huehuetenango Finca Vista Hermosa
coffees.origin: Agua Dulce, San Pedro Necta, Huehuetenango, Guatemala
coffees.process: Washed · 24 to 36 hour ferment · patio dried
coffees.processNote: The Martinez family runs their own wet mill on the farm, which is rarer than you would think and means nobody else touches the coffee between the tree and the bag. Cherries are picked by hand at full ripeness, pulped, fermented in tanks for a day to a day and a half to loosen the fruit, washed clean, and then sun-dried on patios. It is the classic Guatemalan way, done carefully, and it gives you a sweet, malty, balanced cup with a little winey edge, the kind of coffee you can drink all morning.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Finca Vista Hermosa, which means beautiful view farm, is about eight hours by car from Guatemala City in the mountains of Huehuetenango, up near the Mexican border. Edwin Martinez's grandfather started it in the 1950s, when the roads were barely roads, and Edwin, a third generation agronomist, now runs it with his father. The coffee grows on hillsides so steep they call it impossible terrain, up to 1,800 meters, and that steepness creates pockets of microclimate that slow the cherry down and make a denser, sweeter bean. This lot is Bourbon and Caturra, though the farm also grows Catuai and Pacamara because Edwin likes to see what the land can do.

Huehuetenango is the highest and driest coffee country in Guatemala, under the Cuchumatanes, the tallest mountain range in Central America that is not a volcano. Warm dry wind blows up from the Tehuantepec plain in Mexico and keeps frost off the trees, so coffee here can grow higher than almost anywhere else in the country. The Martinez family has agronomists visit every month and opens those sessions up to their neighbors, most of them small Mayan farmers with their own little mills, which is part of why this corner of the mountains has become famous.

journey.label: Finca Vista Hermosa · Huehuetenango, Guatemala
journey.story: Huehuetenango is the far northwest corner of Guatemala, where the mountains pile up against the Mexican border. Finca Vista Hermosa clings to the slopes above the town of San Pedro Necta, on terrain the family calls impossible, and the coffee ripens slowly in the high dry air. To the northeast the Cuchumatanes rise to nearly 3,800 meters, the highest ground in Central America that is not a volcano.

lookArounds.label: Climb the temples of Tikal
lookArounds.note: Tikal National Park, deep in the Petén rainforest in the north of the country. This was one of the great cities of the Maya, home to tens of thousands of people at its height around 1,300 years ago, and Temple IV here is the tallest thing they ever built, over 60 meters of stone rising out of the jungle canopy. Howler monkeys own the soundtrack. It is a full day's drive from the farm, but you did not come this far to skip it.

coldBrew.name: One Batch Cold Brew
coldBrew.aboutFarm:
Origin TBD, but it'll be something worth the wait. Steeped 18 to 24 hours, half a gallon of water to 220 grams of grounds, a ratio strong enough that you're meant to dilute it rather than wonder where the flavor went. What comes out the other end is thick and dark, closer to a concentrate than a coffee, even though nobody around here calls it that.

Cut it with cream and a splash of water if you want it easy. A touch of sweetener if that's your thing, no judgment. Or pour it straight over ice, no water, no cream, and let it hit the way it's supposed to. That's how I drink the first glass of every batch, standing at the counter, deciding if this one's a keeper.

Brewed once, one batch, by the half gallon. When it's gone, it's gone until the next one.
